content.thinking:
Wait, that ran in 0.2s but found 1140 members (all width-3 positive clauses as predicted). But the DFS should have visited ~87K nodes... unless the witnesses pruning cut it. Let me check: negative literals — literal ¬i is true on contexts where atom i is false, i.e., i ∈ F. Per source: pairs containing i = 19 contexts ✓ (S=1) → negative literals are eligible. Then clauses with negative literals: condition 4 for {¬i, ¬j}: witnesses for ¬i = contexts where i ∈ F and j ∉ F → pairs {i,x} with x≠j → exists ✓. So {¬i,¬j} passes condition 4. Condition 3: clause (¬i ∨ ¬j) true on c iff i∈F or j∈F → needs every context's F to contain i or j → false (F is a random pair). So condition 3 fails, but the node is visited and checked, then recursion continues to depth 3, 4...

Hmm, so why only 0.2s? Let me instrument: count DFS nodes visited. Maybe the witnesses check fails fast for mixed clauses at depth 2-3 (the per-source loop breaks early). Let's see: for a mixed clause like {i+, j-}: witnesses for i+ = contexts where atom i true and ¬j true (atom j false) → F contains j but not i → pair {j,x} with x≠i → exists ✓. Witnesses for j- = contexts where j ∈ F and atom i true → F = {j,x}, x≠i... wait, witnesses for ¬j = contexts where ¬j true (j ∈ F) and all other literals false (atom i false → i ∈ F) → F ⊇ {i,j} → F = {i,j} exactly ✓ exists. So mixed pairs pass condition 4. Then depth 3: {i+, j+, k-}: witnesses for k- need F ⊇ {i,j} (both false) and j... i.e. F = {i,j} ✓. witnesses for i+ need F ⊇ {j} (j false), k ∈ F... wait ¬k true means k ∈ F; other literals (i+, j+) false → i,j ∈ F. So witnesses for i+ need i ∉ F but j ∈ F — contradiction with "i+ false"... let me redo: witnesses for literal i+ = contexts where i+ is true and all other literals in the clause are false. i+ true → i ∉ F. j+ false → j ∈ F. k- false → k ∉ F. So F = {j, x} with x ∉ {i,k}. Exists ✓.

So most 3-clauses pass condition 4 regardless of signs. Then the DFS should visit ~87K nodes... unless it prunes via psig == ALLPROBE. AH WAIT — that's it! psig for a clause with positive literals: the clause is true on probe p iff some literal is true there. Probes have ALL atoms false → positive literals are false everywhere on probes; negative literals are TRUE everywhere on probes. So a clause containing any negative literal has psig = ALLPROBE → pruned immediately at the depth where the first negative literal is added! That's why it's fast: only ~all-positive clauses are explored deeply.

So to defeat psig pruning, probes must make each single literal false but combinations... impossible: if all literals are false on a probe, then in particular each literal is false on that probe. Hmm — the pruning condition is `psig == ALLPROBE` meaning the clause is true on ALL probes. For the DFS to not prune, we need every partial clause to be false on at least one probe. 

Let me think about what input maximizes DFS node visits. The pruning happens when a partial clause is true on all probes. To avoid that, we want: for every small set of literals, some probe where all are false. If probes have all-atoms-false, then any clause containing a negative literal is true on all probes → pruned. If instead probes have all-atoms-TRUE, then any clause containing a positive literal is true everywhere on probes → pruned.

We need probes that are diverse: for each literal (or small set), a probe where those atoms have the right values. With 128 probes and 40 literals, we can arrange: for each atom i, a probe where atom i is false (making literal i+ false there) and a probe where atom i is true (making ¬i false there). Then a clause is true on all probes only if... e.g., clause {i+, j+}: true on all probes iff for every probe, i or j true. If there's a probe where both i and j are false → not pruned. With 128 probes and 20 atoms, we can have probes covering many pairs: a probe with false-set F makes all positive literals of atoms in F false and all negative literals of atoms NOT in F false. So a clause C (with signs) is false on probe F iff for each positive literal i+ ∈ C: i ∈ F, and for each negative literal i- ∈ C: i ∉ F.

For no pruning, we want for every clause (subset ≤ 4 with signs) a probe F that "matches" it. With 128 probes we can cover a lot: e.g., probes = 128 random false-sets. A random false-set of size 10 matches a given 4-clause with probability ~(1/2)^4 = 1/16 → with 128 probes, almost surely some probe matches → no pruning for most clauses. 

So: probes = 128 random contexts with ~half the atoms false. Then most clauses are false on some probe → no psig pruning → DFS visits all ~87K nodes → worst case cost. Let me also keep the training structure (all pairs as false-sets, 16 sources) so condition 4 checks pass for most nodes (maximizing work and recorded clauses).

Then the eligible clauses: those passing conditions 3, 4, 5. Width-3 positive clauses: 1140 (as before). Mixed clauses: condition 3 requires coverage of all training contexts. Hmm, for clause {¬i, ¬j}: needs every context to have i ∈ F or j ∈ F → fails. So mixed clauses fail condition 3 but still get checked (cost paid).

So the DFS cost is the dominant factor. Let me build stress3 = training with all pairs per source, probes = 128 random half-false contexts, queries = 1024 random contexts.

Let me measure.

content.text: The all-false probes enabled aggressive pruning. Let me build the real worst case with random probes:

arguments.command:
cd /app/dev && python3 - << 'PYEOF'
import json, random
rng = random.Random(11)
NATOMS, NSRC = 20, 16
schema = [{'name':'f%d'%i,'type':'FLAG'} for i in range(NATOMS)]
atoms = [{'cmp':'eq','left':{'field':'f%d'%i,'at':0},'right':{'const':True,'type':'FLAG'}} for i in range(NATOMS)]
pairs = [(i,j) for i in range(NATOMS) for j in range(i+1,NATOMS)]
def row(fs):
    v=[True]*NATOMS
    for i in fs: v[i]=False
    return v
train=[]; t=0
for s in range(NSRC):
    fs=list(pairs); rng.shuffle(fs)
    extra=[rng.choice(pairs) for _ in range(66)]
    rows=[{'t':t+k,'values':row(f)} for k,f in enumerate(fs+extra)]
    t+=len(rows); train.append({'id':'tr%d'%s,'source':'src%d'%s,'rows':rows})
probes=[{'id':'pr0','source':'src0','rows':[
    {'t':i,'values':row(tuple(sorted(rng.sample(range(NATOMS),10))))} for i in range(128)]}]
queries=[]; t=0
for q in range(4):
    rows=[]
    for c in range(256):
        f=tuple(sorted(rng.sample(range(NATOMS),10)))
        rows.append({'t':t+c,'values':row(f)})
    t+=256; queries.append({'id':'qr%d'%q,'source':'src0','rows':rows})
req={'version':1,'schema':schema,'window':1,'atoms':atoms,
     'policy':{'max_width':4,'min_support':1,'min_witness':1},
     'train':train,'probes':probes,'queries':queries}
json.dump(req,open('stress3.json','w'))
print('written')
PYEOF
cd /app/dev && (time /app/submission/run.sh < stress3.json > out3.json) 2>&1 | tail -4; python3 -c "
import json;r=json.load(open('/app/dev/out3.json'));print('classes',len(r['classes']),'members',sum(c['members'] for c in r['classes']));print('q0',r['queries'][0])"
